claims.text: Protective oxide formation and stability in CrFeCoNiX alloys are governed by grain size.
Protective oxide formation and stability in CrFeCoNiX alloys are governed by the distribution of elements.
Annealing and homogenization can control grain size and elemental distribution.
A finer grain size can produce a more stable and coherent oxide layer.
A more uniform elemental distribution can produce a more stable and coherent oxide layer.
A coarser grain size can produce a less stable oxide layer.
A non-uniform elemental distribution can produce a less stable oxide layer.
Alloys with finer grains and more uniform elemental distributions will have greater high-temperature corrosion resistance than alloys with coarser grains and non-uniform distributions.
The uncontrolled baseline alloy will show intermediate corrosion behavior.
The proposed comparison uses CrFeCoNiX alloys without grain-size control as the baseline.
The proposed exposure is an oxidative atmosphere at 900 °C for up to 100 hours.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to X = Si, Mn, or Al in single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution states.
Weight gain, surface morphology, and oxide-layer thickness can be used to compare corrosion behavior between processed and baseline alloys.
Failure of the grain-size-controlled alloys to improve corrosion resistance over the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
